Friedrich Staphylus
freed'rikh sta'fi-lus
n. (1512–1564; Königsberg professor of theology who returned to Rome and wrote against the Reformation he had taught)
Staphylus, a Greek rendering of the German surname Stapellage or Staffel; from staphule, a bunch of grapes.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Friedrich Staphylus was born in Osnabrück, studied at Wittenberg where he lodged with Melanchthon, and in 1546 became professor of theology at the new university at Königsberg. He was deep in the Prussian church's business for a decade, drafting and disputing. The Osiander controversy broke him: he sided against Osiander, found the duke against him, and in 1552 left for the Empire, where in 1553 he returned to the Church of Rome. Ferdinand I made him an imperial councillor and he spent his last years as a polemicist against the Reformation, arguing from the Lutherans' own divisions that the appeal to Scripture alone must end in endless schism. His Theologiae Martini Lutheri trimembris epitome was answered up and down Germany. The dictionary records him because an apostasy from within the schools is a real event with real arguments, and because Scripture does not flinch from the category: “Now the just shall live by faith: but if any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him” (Heb 10:38).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines apostasy as an abandonment of what one has professed; to recant as to retract a declaration or opinion; and schism as a division in a church or among the members of a religious body.

expand to see more

APOSTASY, n. [Gr. apostasia, a standing away.] An abandonment of what one has professed; a total desertion or departure from one's faith or religion.

RECANT, v.t. [L. recanto.] To retract; to recall; to contradict a former declaration; to unsay.

SCHISM, n. [Gr. schisma, a rent.] A division or separation in a church or religious body; a rent, a cleft.

WITHDRAW, v.t. To take back; to retire; to recall; to draw from a place or from a party.

PROFESS, v.t. [L. profiteor.] To make open declaration of; to avow; to acknowledge one's belief in.

Key Scripture

Heb 10:38 — "Now the just shall live by faith: but if any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him."

2Pe 2:21 — "For it had been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness, than, after they have known it, to turn from the holy commandment delivered unto them."

1Jn 2:19 — "They went out from us, but they were not of us; for if they had been of us, they would no doubt have continued with us: but they went out, that they might be made manifest that they were not all of us."

Luk 9:62 — "And Jesus said unto him, No man, having put his hand to the plough, and looking back, is fit for the kingdom of God."

Modern Corruption

Professor of theology at Königsberg from 1546 who left Prussia in the Osiander crisis, returned to Rome in 1553, and wrote against the Reformation for Ferdinand I.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Staphylus did, however, make an argument still in daily use, and it deserves an answer rather than a sneer. He said: you appealed to Scripture against the church, and within thirty years you were at each other's throats over justification in your own university; therefore the appeal cannot stand, and authority must rest somewhere visible. He had watched the Osiandrist quarrel from the inside and he was not inventing the mess. The answer is not that the divisions were small. It is that a true thing is not disproved by the quarrels of those who hold it, and that Rome's own history of contested councils and rival popes rules out the comparison he wanted.

The principle to recover is that drawing back is a real possibility held out as a warning to professors of religion, not an abstraction: “Now the just shall live by faith: but if any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him” (Heb 10:38). Peter puts the aggravation plainly — it is worse to have known the way of righteousness and turn from it (2Pe 2:21) — and John reads the departure backwards, as evidence about what the man was all along: “They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1Jn 2:19). The Lord's own word is about the direction a man is facing while his hand is on the work (Luk 9:62).

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek hupostello (G5288), to draw back or shrink; Greek epistrepho (G1994), to turn back.

expand to see more

Greek hupostello (G5288) — to draw back, to shrink from, to withdraw; Hebrews 10:38.

Greek epistrepho (G1994) — to turn about, to turn back; “to turn from the holy commandment”, 2 Peter 2:21.

Greek meno (G3306) — to abide, to continue, to remain; “they would no doubt have continued with us”, 1 John 2:19.

Greek euthetos (G2111) — well placed, fit, suitable; “is fit for the kingdom of God”, Luke 9:62.

Greek apostasia (G646) — a defection, a falling away; the root behind the English apostasy.

Usage

"“Now the just shall live by faith” (Heb 10:38) — professor of theology at Königsberg, 1546."

"“but if any man draw back, my soul shall have no pleasure in him” (Heb 10:38) — returned to the Church of Rome in 1553."

"“They went out from us, but they were not of us” (1Jn 2:19) — imperial councillor and polemicist against the Reformation."
